name: Debt consolidation
seoDesc: Debt consolidation: work out total debt from the balance #1 and the balance #2. A free finance calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Give the Debt consolidation calculator the balance #1, the balance #2, the interest rate #1 and the interest rate #2 and it returns total debt. It is built for a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Debt consolidation calculator work?
sections.html:
The Debt consolidation calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports total debt in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (number of debts, the type of payments and the payment type boxes (numbered 1 to 6)); then you give the first due date; then you type in the balance boxes (numbered 1 to 6), the interest rate boxes (numbered 1 to 7), the payment boxes (numbered 1 to 6) and the loan term.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

sections.title: The formula behind the Debt consolidation calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Total debt=(balance #1, balance #2, balance #3, balance #4, balance #5, balance #6, vardebt)
Debt consolidation=(balance #1, balance #2, balance #3, balance #4, balance #5, balance #6, payment #1, payment #2, payment #3, payment #4, payment #5, payment #6, interest rate #1, interest rate #2, interest rate #3, interest rate #4, interest rate #5, interest rate #6, Vart 1, Vart 2, Vart 3, Vart 4, Vart 5, Vart 6, first due date, vardebt, varpmttype, varconamount, varrep, loan amount, loaned fee, prepaid fee, interest rate, loan term)
Debt total=()
Con loan=()
Debt apr=()
Con apr=()

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Balance #1: Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • Interest rate #1: %, opening in percent
  • Payment #1: Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • Balance #2: Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • Interest rate #2: %, opening in percent
  • Payment #2: Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • Balance #3: Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • Interest rate #3: %, opening in percent

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Debt consolidation calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Preparing questions for a lender, an accountant or an adviser
  • Sizing up a purchase before you commit to it
  • Building a monthly budget and testing how one number shifts the rest
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the balance #1, the balance #2 and the interest rate #1 — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Dates are compared date to date in your own time zone, so a daylight-saving change will not shift the count by a day.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Debt consolidation calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns total debt, derived from the balance #1, the balance #2 and the interest rate #1. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Debt consolidation calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the balance #1, the balance #2, the interest rate #1 and the interest rate #2, which is 36 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter balance #1 in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Balance #1 opens in US Dollar and the chip beside it offers 113 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (10 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Varpmttype = 0. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Debt consolidation calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
